title: MRI-based radiomics with SHAP interpretation for preoperative prediction of upstaging in ductal carcinoma in situ : a comparative study of intratumoral, peritumoral, habitat, and fusion models.
abstract: Background Preoperative prediction of upstaging in ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is crucial to avoid unnecessary sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in low-risk patients. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based radiomics model for this purpose and to systematically compare the predictive value of intratumoral, peritumoral, and habitat-based features. Methods This retrospective study included 108 women with biopsy-proven DCIS. Radiomics features were extracted from intratumoral and peritumoral regions (2, 4, 6 mm) on dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI. Six models (clinical, intratumoral, peritumoral, habitat, feature-fusion, image-fusion) were developed and compared using multiple machine learning classifiers. The best-performing model was validated on an independent test set (n=33). Model interpretability was achieved using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results The image-fusion model integrating intratumoral and 2-mm peritumoral features showed promising performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.892 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.817-0.967] in the training set and 0.864 (95% CI: 0.735-0.992) in the test set. SHAP analysis identified textural heterogeneity as a key predictor. Using predefined radiomics score (Rad-score) thresholds derived from the training set, the high-sensitivity threshold achieved a negative predictive value of 100% (10/10) and the high-specificity threshold achieved a positive predictive value of 61.5% (8/13) in the independent test set. An exploratory ultra-low-risk threshold (Rad-score <0.25) identified a subgroup of 5 out of 33 patients (15.2%) with no upstaging. Conclusions The proposed MRI-based radiomics model may assist in preoperative risk stratification for DCIS upstaging, but these findings are exploratory and require prospective multicenter validation.

title: Radiomics-based machine learning models decipher heterogeneity of anoikis-related molecular subtypes for prognostic stratification in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Background Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) exhibits high molecular heterogeneity and frequent metastasis, which is strongly linked to anoikis dysregulation. This study aimed to investigate whether radiomics could offer a novel perspective for assessing the heterogeneity and risk stratification of HNSC associated with anoikis-related genes (ANRGs). Methods A total of 118 HNSC patients with paired gene expression and imaging data were included. Radiomics features were extracted from computed tomography (CT) images using PyRadiomics. By employing consensus clustering methods, the heterogeneity of ANRGs-related HNSC was identified into different subtypes, and multi-machine learning model combinations were constructed based on radiomics features to predict the molecular subtypes. An ANRGs-related radiomics prognostic model was constructed to assess the association between subtypes and clinical outcomes. Results Three subtypes were identified via consensus clustering of 31 prognostic ANRG expression profiles: C1, C2, and C3. Compared to other subtypes, C1 exhibited significantly worse overall survival and distinct immune infiltration levels. Of the multi-combination machine learning models, 71% demonstrated robust generalization in predicting C1 [areas under the curve (AUC) >0.75). The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator-random forest combined model achieved optimal performance, with an AUC of 0.86. The ANRGs-associated radiomics prognostic model showed significant prognostic value and was closely linked to pathways involving enhanced tumor invasiveness and immunosuppressive microenvironment. Conclusions This study demonstrated that radiomics enables stratified prediction of ANRGs-associated HNSC heterogeneity while providing molecular annotation and prognostic evaluation for ANRGs-related radiomics features, highlighting its translational value in precision oncology.

title: MRI-derived habitat radiomics integrated with transformer deep learning for preoperative prediction of high CD9 expression: a novel prognostic marker in adult-type diffuse gliomas.
abstract: Background High CD9 expression is significantly associated with shorter overall survival (OS) in patients with adult-type diffuse gliomas (ADGs). Concurrently, drug screening analyses have identified emetine as a potential targeted therapeutic agent for gliomas exhibiting high CD9 expression, indicating that CD9 may serve as a novel biomarker with the potential to transform glioma diagnosis and treatment. This study aimed to develop an artificial intelligence prediction model based on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images to facilitate the early identification of high CD9 expression in patients with ADGs. Methods We retrospectively collected CD9 expression data from 262 patients with ADGs in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA) cohorts. Using preoperative MRI sequences [contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging (CET1) and T2-weighted imaging (T2WI)], Habitat features were extracted, using K-means clustering algorithm, together with radiomic features. Additionally, multi-channel 2.5-dimensional deep learning (2.5D_DL) data were constructed, based on neural network architectures, including ResNet101, DenseNet121, and SimpleViT, and DL features were extracted. Seven classifiers were utilized to construct individual Radiomics, Habitat, and 2.5D_DL predictive models. Subsequently, a Stacking model was developed via an ensemble fusion strategy to predict high CD9 expression. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, and clinical efficacy was assessed by decision curve analysis (DCA). Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to explore the interpretation of the models, enhancing the transparency of the machine learning predictions. In addition, Patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups based on Stacking model scores, and survival differences were compared using the Kaplan-Meier analysis and the log-rank test. Results The Habitat model exhibited superior ROC curve [area under the ROC (AUC)] values than the Radiomics model. Among the multi-channel 2.5D_DL models, the SimpleViT model achieved slightly better performance than the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based models (ResnNet101 and DenseNet121). The final Stacking model, which integrated the outputs from Habitat, Radiomics, and 2.5D_DL models exhibited superior AUC values. The AUC reached 0.999, 0.822, and 0.728 in the training, validation, and test sets, respectively. DeLong testing confirmed the statistically significant differences in the AUC values of each model in the training set, but no statistically significant differences were observed among the other sets. In addition, enhanced net clinical benefit across a more extensive range of risk thresholds for this integrated model was verified by DCA. Prognostic stratification by Stacking model revealed significant differences in survival outcomes between high-risk and low-risk groups. Conclusions The preoperative MRI-based Stacking model effectively identifies patients with high CD9 expression among ADGs and stratifies patient risk, providing support for clinical therapeutic decision-making and individualized prognostic evaluation. Prospective multicenter data are still required to validate the prognostic performance and generalizability of this model.

title: Pulmonary metastasectomy and response-adapted preoperative surveillance in resectable metastatic osteosarcoma: a single-center retrospective cohort study with long-term follow-up.
abstract: Background Pulmonary metastasectomy remains the standard of care for resectable metastatic osteosarcoma. However, controversy persists regarding minimally invasive surgery versus thoracotomy for occult nodule detection, the optimal use and duration of preoperative systemic therapy and prognostic factors associated with long-term survival. This study aimed to evaluate surgical approaches, assess the use and duration of preoperative systemic therapy, and identify prognostic factors associated with long-term survival in this population. Methods At a single center, we retrospectively reviewed 159 patients who underwent 229 pulmonary metastasectomies from 2000 to 2022. Eligible patients had pathologically confirmed osteosarcoma, resectable pulmonary metastatic disease, surgery intended to remove all known lesions and postoperative follow-up. The primary endpoint was post-metastasis survival (PMS), defined from metastatic diagnosis to death or the last follow-up. Computed tomography (CT) was scheduled every 4-8 weeks during preoperative surveillance and at prespecified postoperative intervals. Surgical approaches included conventional thoracotomy, mini-thoracotomy, and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). Preoperative strategies comprised upfront surgery or preoperative systemic therapy with first- or second-line chemotherapy, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), or their combination. Oncological and perioperative outcomes were analyzed with a median follow-up of 79.1 months. Results The median age was 17.0 years, 106 (66.7%) patients were male, and 185 of 229 procedures (80.8%) followed preoperative systemic therapy. The 3- and 5-year PMS were 52.2% and 36.0%, respectively. Despite advances in CT resolution, palpation-assisted mini-thoracotomy identified more occult lesions than VATS (43.4% vs. 6.8%, P=0.004), with comparable rates of surgical complications. However, no significant difference in survival was observed between mini-thoracotomy and VATS. Remarkably, response to preoperative systemic therapy was the strongest independent predictor of survival, with a 5-year survival rate of 41.1% in responders versus 0.0% in non-responders (hazard ratio =0.22, P<0.001). Responders also exhibited a trend toward higher immune diversity (P=0.055) and increased CD8 + T cell infiltration (P=0.098) in metastasectomy specimens. Using tumor response modeling, we identified a 2-3-month period as the optimal duration for preoperative surveillance. Conclusions In this single-center retrospective cohort, preoperative surveillance and response-adapted strategy, combined with palpation-assisted mini-thoracotomy, was associated with favorable long-term outcomes of metastasectomy in patients with resectable metastatic osteosarcoma. However, given the observational design and modest sample size, these findings are exploratory and require validation in larger multicenter prospective studies.

title: Interpretable deep learning and radiomics for predicting the occurrence of brain metastases following prophylactic brain irradiation in small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Background Brain metastasis remains an important clinical concern in patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC), even after prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI). Accurate identification of patients at high risk of brain metastasis after PCI may facilitate individualized surveillance and management. This study developed a fusion model based on two-and-a-half-dimensional (2.5D) multi-channel deep learning features, clinical features, and radiomics features to predict whether patients with SCLC will develop brain metastases following PCI. Methods This retrospective study included 185 patients with SCLC who underwent PCI and randomly divided them into a training set (N=148) and a testing set (N=37). A 2.5D multi-channel convolutional neural network (CNN) model was constructed based on multi-planar regions of interest (ROI) derived from CT images to extract 2.5D deep learning features. Based on the largest cross-section and three-dimensional (3D) volume of the tumor ROI, two-dimensional (2D) and 3D deep learning features were extracted, respectively. Subsequently, features from different dimensions were fused with clinical features and traditional omics features to construct the 2D_clinic_Rad, 2.5D_clinic_Rad, and 3D_clinic_Rad models, respectively. The performance differences between the 3D models and the clinical and traditional radiomics models were then compared. Results The 2.5D_clinic_Rad fusion model demonstrated the best performance in predicting brain metastases, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.841 on the test set, outperforming clinical models, traditional radiomics models, and 2D and 3D deep learning fusion models. Analysis of decision curves and calibration curves indicated that the 2.5D_clinic_Rad model demonstrated the highest clinical net benefit and the best calibration consistency compared to other models. Conclusions The fusion model based on 2.5D_clinic_Rad can effectively predict the risk of brain metastasis in patients with SCLC following whole-brain prophylactic irradiation.

title: AI agents in cancer imaging: Concepts, advances, and clinical perspectives.
abstract: Medical imaging serves as a critical source of evidence for cancer diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. However, most existing medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI) systems still operate on predefined tasks and inputs, limiting their ability to address the evolving needs of clinical practice and research. AI agents use foundation models as central engines for reasoning and orchestration. They organize analytical processes according to task objectives, invoke external tools and data resources, and adapt subsequent actions based on intermediate results. They may therefore facilitate a shift in cancer imaging AI from isolated model applications toward continuous workflow support. This review outlines the fundamental principles, system components, and evaluation approaches for AI agents from a cancer imaging perspective and summarizes representative advances in image interpretation, clinical decision support, and research workflows. Current evidence suggests that agents can connect previously fragmented imaging, clinical, and knowledge resources, thereby potentially improving the continuity and traceability of complex tasks. Nevertheless, clinical evidence for AI agents remains limited, as most studies have been conducted in controlled settings and have yet to demonstrate consistent value in real-world clinical workflows. Clinical translation is further constrained by the computational demands and potential error propagation inherent in multistep execution, as well as by the dependence of agent performance on specific tools, data environments, and workflow configurations. Future research should move beyond task-level performance toward system-level validation, with particular emphasis on whether agents can reliably organize information, interpret findings, and collaborate effectively with clinicians. Such evidence will be essential to clarify their practical role in cancer imaging care and research.

Nevertheless, clinical evidence for AI agents remains limited, as most studies have been conducted in controlled settings and have yet to demonstrate consistent value in real-world clinical workflows. Clinical translation is further constrained by the computational demands and potential error propagation inherent in multistep execution, as well as by the dependence of agent performance on specific tools, data environments, and workflow configurations. Future research should move beyond task-level performance toward system-level validation, with particular emphasis on whether agents can reliably organize information, interpret findings, and collaborate effectively with clinicians. Such evidence will be essential to clarify their practical role in cancer imaging care and research.

title: SRM-UNet: A Lightweight Structure-Region Guided Network with Multi-Receptive-Field Learning for Dermoscopic Skin Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Accurate skin lesion segmentation remains challenging because of blurred boundaries, low contrast, irregular lesion morphology, and interference from surrounding textures. This paper presents SRM-UNet, a lightweight structure-region guided network with multi-receptive-field learning for dermoscopic skin lesion segmentation. The central design of SRM-UNet is an explicit structure-region prior collaboration mechanism between the encoder and decoder. Specifically, the Structure-aware Local-Global Encoder (SLGE) performs stage-adaptive multi-receptive-field modeling and generates scale-matched structure priors that encode boundary, texture-transition, and shape-related cues. Prior-guided Refinement after Fusion (PRSF) refines decoder features after skip-feature fusion by coupling decoder-derived region priors for lesion localization with encoder-derived structure priors for boundary and shape correction. In this way, the generated priors provide explicit guidance for region-dominant and structure-assisted feature refinement. Auxiliary region supervision and boundary supervision are incorporated during training to improve intermediate lesion localization and contour-aware feature learning. Experiments were conducted on the ISIC2017, ISIC2018, and PH2 datasets. SRM-UNet achieved Dice/mIoU scores of 0.8441/0.7303, 0.8790/0.7841 , and 0.9267/0.8634 on ISIC2017, ISIC2018, and PH2, respectively, with 0.052 M parameters and 0.265 GFLOPs. These results indicate that SRM-UNet achieves a favorable balance between segmentation accuracy and model complexity, particularly for challenging lesions with blurred contours, low contrast, and irregular shapes. Overall, SRM-UNet provides a compact prior-guided segmentation framework for resource-constrained dermoscopic image analysis. The source code is publicly available on GitHub to support reproducibility.

title: Ultrasound-guided bilateral Erector Spinae Plane Block, bilateral quadratus lumborum block, and lumbar epidural for postoperative analgesia in patients undergoing total abdominal hysterectomy: a prospective randomized clinical trial
abstract: Abstract Background Open total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH) is commonly followed by considerable postoperative pain. Although epidural analgesia (EA) has traditionally been used as a standard technique, peripheral regional blocks may offer effective alternatives. This trial compared the analgesic performance of the transmuscular quadratus lumborum block (TQLB), erector spinae plane block (ESPB), and lumbar epidural block (LEB) in women undergoing open TAH for gynecological malignancy. Methods This prospective randomized controlled trial enrolled 90 patients scheduled for elective TAH under general anesthesia. Participants were allocated equally to three groups: the TQLB group received bilateral type-3 QLB, the ESPB group received bilateral ESPB, and the LEB group received a lumbar epidural block (30 patients per group). The primary endpoint was cumulative morphine use during the first 24 postoperative hours. Secondary endpoints included the duration of analgesia, intraoperative fentanyl requirements, and postoperative pain intensity. Results Twenty-four-hour morphine consumption was significantly lower with TQLB than with ESPB or LEB (p < 0.001) and was also lower with ESPB than with LEB. Analgesia lasted significantly longer in the TQLB group than in the other two groups (p < 0.001), while ESPB provided a longer duration than LEB (p = 0.028). During the first 8 hours, pain scores were lower in the TQLB and ESPB groups than in the LEB group. From 12 to 24 hours, TQLB produced lower pain scores than both ESPB and LEB. Hemodynamic stability was maintained with all three techniques. Conclusion Bilateral TQLB performed at L2 and bilateral ESPB performed at T10 provide effective postoperative analgesia and reduce morphine requirements in patients with gynecological cancer undergoing open TAH under general anesthesia. TQLB was associated with the longest analgesic duration. Trial registration The trial was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06397300; registration date: 18 April 2024). As for the WHO trial registry: https://trialsearch.who.int/Trial2.aspx?TrialID=NCT06397300

title: Dosimetric Evaluation of CBCT-Guided Setup errors and Adaptive Radiotherapy Replanning in Proton Therapy for Lung Cancer
abstract: Abstract Background To investigate the dosimetric impact of setup errors in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-guided proton therapy for lung cancer and to evaluate the role of adaptive radiotherapy (ART) based on a sequential adaptive planning approach for maintaining optimal dose distribution after reductions in target volume. Methods Patients with lung cancer who underwent proton radiotherapy at our institution between April 2024 and January 2026 were retrospectively evaluated. The first cohort (n = 29) received treatment according to the original plan throughout the entire course. CBCT images acquired during each treatment session were used to calculate mean setup deviations in the X, Y, and Z directions. These average shifts were applied to generate simulated treatment plans, and dosimetric parameters for the CTV and OARs were compared with those of the original plans. In the second group of patients (n = 17), one adaptive radiotherapy intervention was implemented during treatment. The initial treatment plan was termed Plan00. Following the detection of significant target shrinkage on CBCT, a repeat CT scan was acquired. The dose delivered before replanning was recorded as Plan01, while a revised plan (Plan1) was developed using the new CT dataset. After dose registration and accumulation of Plan01 and Plan1, the resulting dose-volume metrics were compared with those of Plan00 to evaluate the dosimetric impact of adaptive replanning relative to a non-adaptive treatment strategy. Changes in dosimetric parameters were analyzed, including lung V 5 , V 20 and D mean , spinal cord D 1cc and D max , esophageal V5, and D mean . Results Average setup errors along the X, Y, and Z axes were 0.08 ± 2.71 mm, 0.53 ± 0.36 mm, and 0.23 ± 1.03 mm, respectively, with maximum absolute deviations of 14 mm, 29 mm, and 14 mm. The greatest positioning variability was observed in the Y direction, where 7% of errors exceeded 5 mm. Errors ≤ 3 mm occurred in 81.5%, 76.6%, and 93.3% of fractions, whereas errors ≤ 5 mm were observed in 99.0%, 92.8%, and 94.5% of fractions for the X, Y, and Z axes, respectively. Compared with the simulated plan, the original plan achieved 104.31% ± 14.41%, 102.23% ± 11.40%, 98.84% ± 9.37%, and 100.26% ± 9.66% of the corresponding CTV D 98% , D 95% , D 2%, and D mean values, respectively. Ratios for spinal cord D 1cc , spinal cord D max , lung V 5 , lung V 20 , bilateral lung D mean , esophageal V 5 , and heart D mean were 90.60% ± 24.05%, 87.23% ± 21.57%, 91.11% ± 45.12%, 101.01% ± 36.17%, 100.22 ± 14.46%, 105.50% ± 20.36%, and 102.15% ± 22.05%, respectively. The simulated plan showed significantly lower CTV D9 8%, D 95% , and D mean values than the original plan (all P < 0.01). In the adaptive radiotherapy cohort, GTV decreased from 132 ± 104 cm 3 on the initial planning CT to 97 ± 69 cm 3 on the repeat CT, representing a mean reduction of 35 ± 55 cm 3 . This reduction was statistically significant (t = 2.54, P < 0.05). Relative to the non-adaptive plan (Plan00), adaptive replanning (Plan01 + Plan1) significantly reduced lungV5 (35.53 ± 12.36% versus 32.36 ± 12.77%), lung V 20 (20.66 ± 8.14% versus 17.47 ± 7.78%), and whole-lung D mean (6.26 ± 2.98 GyE versus 5.33 ± 2.78 GyE) (all P < 0.01). Heart V 30 decreased from 8.36 ± 14.84% to 4.22 ± 3.89%, and spinal cord D max decreased from 23.04 ± 15.61 GyE to 21.55 ± 13.59 GyE; however, neither difference was statistically significant (P > 0.05). Conclusion Proton therapy is highly susceptible to setup uncertainties and anatomical variations during treatment. CBCT-guided image verification plays a critical role in maintaining treatment accuracy for lung cancer. Adaptive replanning based on imaging-detected changes may help preserve target dose coverage while further reducing radiation exposure to OARs.

title: Auditable agentic AI for evidence-grounded thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting
abstract: Abstract Thyroid ultrasound diagnosis requires coordinated lesion localization, measurement, risk stratification and reporting, yet most AI systems address these tasks in isolation and provide limited support for clinical review. We present ThyroidXAgent, a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores their outputs as an auditable case-level evidence record. The system was developed using OpenThyroidDB, a multicentre, multitask resource integrating approximately 0.3 million ultrasound images and 24,000 paired reports, and was evaluated on 28,458 non-overlapping test cases, including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort. Across heterogeneous datasets, ThyroidXAgent achieved a mean Dice score of 87.21% for nodule segmentation and a mean AUROC of 0.9466 for benign–malignant classification. The same workflow supported lymph-node metastasis prediction and follicular versus papillary thyroid carcinoma classification, with AUROCs of 0.864 and 0.805, respectively. For report generation, evidence-grounded assembly outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts. ThyClinScore, a lesion-level clinical semantic metric introduced here, showed the strongest correlation with a location-aware language-model judge. ThyroidXAgent improved physician classification accuracy, increased report diagnostic consistency from 70.3% to 86.2%, and reduced segmentation and reporting time by 35.9% and 27.4%, respectively. These findings support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting.

title: Visual distinctiveness drives memorization beyond rarity in fine-tuned medical imaging models
abstract: Abstract Medical AI models trained on patient data can memorize individual samples,exposing them to membership inference attacks. Long-tail theory predicts rareexamples require memorization, yet rarity alone is insufficient: in a skin-lesiondataset, the rarest class is less vulnerable than the commoner ones. Under ran-domly initialised (MAE) and medical-image-pretrained (MedSAM) encoders,the rarest class stays most memorized, but ImageNet- and vision–language-pretrained encoders re-rank the tail toward visually distinctive classes. Across fivedatasets, controlled grayscale manipulation gives causal evidence: the same trans-form produces opposite effects on two equally rare classes, and an independentfeature-space atypicality measure predicts memorization across architectures.Memorization predicts membership inference vulnerability (ρ = 0.36–0.77,p < 0.001), and medical-domain pretraining (MedSAM, BiomedCLIP) does notreduce rare-class risk. DP-LoRA at ε = 1 reduces the most vulnerable class’s memorization by 90% versus a LoRA-only baseline, with modest accuracy coston simple tasks. We release medmem, an open-source memorization-auditing tool.

title: Development of an automated, reliable, and clinically meaningful artificial intelligence (AI) tool for diagnosing cardiac disease from conventional cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) images
abstract: Abstract Aims Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging enables non-invasive assessment of myocardial structure, function, and pathology, but requires substantial experience in interpretation of CMR images that could be supported by artificial intelligence (AI)-based models. However, use of AI models for enhanced CMR reading is limited by labor-intensive data curation, suboptimal model performance, and unclear implementation pathways. Methods and results We developed an automated data curation pipeline for CMR-based cardiovascular disease (CVD) diagnosis, integrating open-source locally-run large language models (LLMs) to extract diagnostic labels from narrative CMR reports and preprocessing multimodal imaging data, including cine and late-gadolinium-enhancement (LGE) CMR sequences. Three vision foundation models (DINO, VST, UMedPT) were fine-tuned across these modalities in a two-stage approach. The dataset comprised hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM), cardiac amyloidosis (CA), and normal controls (NOR). A total of 988 curated cases were randomly divided into 742 for training and 246 for validation. Fine-tuned AI-models achieved high discriminative diagnostic performance on an independent test set comprising 1067 patients , with individual AUC-ROC values of up to 0.937 for the correct diagnosis of HCM and 0.945 for cardiac amyloidosis. Ensemble strategies combining multiple models and modalities further improved AI-based diagnostic accuracy and robustness, achieving the highest overall diagnostic performance for HCM (AUC=0.959, CI [0.936-0.978]), CA (AUC=0.966, CI [0.939-0.986]), NOR (AUC=0.872, CI [0.852-0.894]), DCM (AUC=0.848, CI [0.808-0.885]) and ICM (AUC=0.840, CI [0.809-0.868]). Conclusions This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that foundation model–based AI methods, when combined with automated report-based curation and multimodal CMR integration, can provide accurate, interpretable, and equitable AI-assisted cardiac diagnosis – and thereby support clinicians in correct interpretation of CMR findings.

title: The AIDE/OBS Study: an international multicenter protocol for AI-ready clinical and intraoperative visual data collection in non-elective minimally invasive surgery for complicated diverticulitis
abstract: Abstract Background The choice between primary colorectal anastomosis and Hartmann’s procedure in non-elective surgery for complicated acute diverticulitis remains a challenging and highly variable decision. Although primary anastomosis is increasingly supported in selected patients, operative strategy is still influenced by patient physiology, disease severity, intraoperative findings, surgeon judgment, institutional culture, and perceived risk of anastomotic failure. This variability makes complicated diverticulitis a clinically relevant model for exploring whether standardized clinical and intraoperative visual data may support future artificial intelligence-assisted decision-making in emergency surgery. Methods The AIDE/OBS study is an international, multicenter, observational, non-interventional study designed to collect standardized clinical, radiological, operative, surgeon-reported, and intraoperative visual data from adult patients undergoing non-elective minimally invasive surgery for complicated acute diverticulitis, classified according to the WSES CT-based classification. Eligible procedures include laparoscopic or robotic Hartmann’s procedure and sigmoidectomy or left colectomy with primary anastomosis, with or without diverting stoma. Participating centers will collect pseudonymized clinical data through a predefined electronic case report form and submit anonymized intraoperative videos or still images, according to predefined decision-relevant surgical phases. Outcomes The primary outcome is the creation of a standardized, annotated, multimodal clinical-visual dataset suitable for descriptive and exploratory analysis of intraoperative decision-making. Feasibility will be assessed through clinical data completeness, availability of analyzable visual material, surgical phase documentation, proportion of complete multimodal cases, and inter-center variability. Secondary outcomes include clinical, radiological, operative, visual, and surgeon-reported factors associated with primary anastomosis versus Hartmann’s procedure, as well as postoperative outcomes including anastomotic leak, morbidity, stoma creation, reoperation, length of stay, and 30-day mortality. Conclusions The AIDE/OBS study will evaluate whether AI-ready clinical and intraoperative visual data can be collected reproducibly across centers in non-elective minimally invasive surgery for complicated diverticulitis. By creating a structured multimodal dataset, the study may provide the methodological foundation for future machine-learning and computer-vision tools aimed at supporting more explicit, reproducible, and data-informed intraoperative decision-making in emergency colorectal surgery. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07651072

title: Do Pathology Foundation Models Learn Biology? Uncertainty-Based Evaluation on AML Cytomorphology
abstract: Abstract Pathology foundation models are increasingly deployed as feature extractors for medical image analysis, yet their advantage over general-purpose vision models in unsupervised settings has not been directly tested. We held the clustering pipeline fixed and varied only the backbone across three pretraining regimes on the AML-Cytomorphology LMU dataset (17,447 single-c cell types): ResNet50 (supervised, ImageNet), DINOv2-large (self-supervised, natural images), and Virchow2 (self-supervised, 3.1 million pathology whole-slide images). Per-cell uncertainty scores served as a probe of biological structure. Virchow2 uncertainty differed substantially across cell types (Kruskal-Wallis H = 178.2, p = 1.5 × 10 −30 ), with transitional myeloid precursors showing higher uncertainty than mature stable types (Ω¯ = 0.384 vs. 0.313, p = 4.3 × 10 −15 ). DINOv2 and ResNet50 showed no such pattern. DINOv2 ranked first on all internal clustering metrics (Silhouette=0.522) yet last on biological recovery (ARI=0.033); Virchow2 showed the inverse ordering. Across five seeds, Virchow2 clustering accuracy fluctuated widely (ARI=0.016 ± 0.006) while its uncertainty structure remained stable, identifying uncertainty as the more reliable signal of representation quality.

title: Target Relocalization-Driven Weakly Supervised Segmentation for Crohn's Disease via Auxiliary Anatomical Priors
abstract: Abstract Background: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory granulomatous condition, and accurate lesion segmentation plays a vital role in improving diagnostic efficiency while reducing the workload of physicians. However, fully supervised medical image segmentation methods depend heavily on large amounts of labeled data, which is particularly costly for the multi-lesion nature of Crohn's disease. Methods: To address this challenge, we propose a method that utilizes image-level annotations to reduce annotation costs while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. Our approach introduces a target re-localization mechanism for Crohn's disease segmentation. While classification networks trained with image-level annotations can generate pseudo-labels, they often suffer from high false-positive rates due to spurious correlations between foreground lesions and background structures ( e.g. , the small intestine). To mitigate this, we incorporate an auxiliary dataset comprising anatomical structures prone to false positives but lacking Crohn's lesions. This auxiliary dataset helps leverage domain-specific anatomical priors, improving the quality of pseudo-labels without additional labeling effort. In addition, classification networks typically focus on the most discriminative parts of the target regions. To expand their attention to the entire target area, we introduce a target re-localization mechanism that allows the network to progressively enlarge its focus. To prevent attention regions from expanding into the background, we integrate a clustering-based metric learning approach, which enhances the accuracy of pseudo-label generation. These pseudo-labels serve as supervisory signals for the segmentation network. Results: Our method achieves a 3.31% improvement in Dice score compared to a mixed dataset. Additionally, the inclusion of all three evaluation metrics significantly enhances model accuracy by 15.52% over individual metrics. Conclusions: Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our approach in Crohn's disease segmentation.

title: From Reconstruction to Interpretation: Zero-Setup Multi-Phase Segmentation of X-ray Tomography Data
abstract: Abstract X-ray tomography enables the nondestructive characterization of materials, and recent advances in micro-CT imaging technology have accelerated the acquisition and reconstruction of volumetric data. However, rapid scientific interpretation remains limited by image segmentation, which typically requires manual thresholding, user prompting, or material-specific model training before meaningful analysis can begin. We present a zero-setup deployment framework for multi-phase segmentation of synchrotron X-ray tomography data that produces interpretable segmentations of previously unseen tomography datasets without user prompting or additional retraining during deployment. The framework combines a material-agnostic mask preparation strategy based on common structural concepts in tomography data such as background, sample, bright regions, dark-gray regions, light-gray regions, and porosity, with a pretrained semantic segmentation network to generate diagnostic-quality segmentations within minutes of reconstruction. Unlike conventional deep learning pipelines that require dataset-specific annotations and retraining, the proposed approach can be applied immediately to new scans, enabling rapid assessment of experimental quality and preliminary microstructural analysis during ongoing beamline experiments. Users can subsequently refine or fine-tune the generated masks when application-specific segmentation is required. Experiments on held-out and qualitatively evaluated synchrotron micro-CT datasets suggest that the framework produces consistent and physically meaningful segmentations on new tomography datasets while substantially outperforming conventional intensity-based thresholding. By bridging the gap between high-speed data acquisition and immediate interpretation, the proposed framework enables near real-time beamline feedback and provides a practical foundation for scalable AI-assisted scientific imaging workflows.

title: Maxilla vs. Mandible: A Multi-Dimensional Risk Scoring System for Dental Implant Planning
abstract: Abstract Background Posterior maxillary and mandibular implant sites carry site-specific anatomical risk profiles that remain inconsistently quantified in pre-operative planning. We developed a multi-dimensional, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based risk scoring system for side-by-side comparison of residual bone quantity and anatomical risk factors between the two jaws. Methods A single-center retrospective cohort of 200 implant sites (100 maxillary, 100 mandibular; consecutively screened adults, both sexes, age 18–79) was analyzed. For each site, residual bone height and width, and jaw-specific anatomical risks (sinus pneumatization, septa, and membrane thickening in the maxilla; lingual undercut depth in the mandible) were scored and summed into a total site risk score (range 0–10). Intra-observer reliability was assessed at a 15-day interval using the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC; single-rater, absolute-agreement, two-way random). Inter-group differences were tested using Welch's t-test or Mann–Whitney U; categorical comparisons used Fisher's exact test for sparse 2×2 tables (cell expectations ≤ 5) and chi-square otherwise. Results Total site risk was approximately two-fold higher in maxillary than in mandibular sites (mean 6.67 ± 2.58 vs 3.40 ± 0.92; p < 0.001, Welch). Risk categories were distributed asymmetrically: 46% of maxillary sites were high or very-high-risk versus 0% of mandibular sites (Fisher exact p < 0.001, two-tailed). Sinus pneumatization emerged as the dominant anatomical risk driver in the maxilla (Pearson r = 0.877 with total risk, p < 0.001). Intra-observer reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.998; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.997–0.999). Conclusions The proposed multi-dimensional scoring system reproducibly distinguishes quantitatively higher risks in posterior maxillary sites, providing an evidence-based, anatomically-anchored case-identification tool for pre-operative planning. Limitations include single-examiner, intra-observer agreement rather than inter-rater calibration and the absence of validated outcome data; future multi-rater, multi-center validation against 1-, 3-, and 5-year implant outcomes is required before this framework can be used as a prognostic index. Clinical trial registration Not applicable.

title: How errors from prompt-assisted longitudinal tumour segmentation change RECIST 1.1 target-lesion response categories: a retrospective out-of-fold analysis
abstract: Abstract Background : RECIST 1.1 requires clinicians to compare target-lesion measurements across examinations. Automated segmentation may support this task, but omission, tracking, persistence, and measurement errors need not affect response equally. We asked how often these errors changed target-lesion response and whether changes favoured apparent benefit. Methods : We retrospectively analysed 258 response-evaluable patients from a public longitudinal whole-body CT cohort with expert per-lesion masks. LongiSeg received the baseline CT, expert baseline mask and an interior location click, plus the follow-up CT and a location click; the expert follow-up mask was withheld. We compared a RECIST 1.1 target-lesion response based on expert masks with one based on expert baseline and model follow-up masks. Each patient was processed by a held-out-fold checkpoint not fitted to that patient. Shapley attribution divided disagreements among prompted omission, tracking mislocalization, false persistence, and measurement (sizing) error. Omission and mislocalization were combined as detection/localization. We estimated disagreement with a Wilson CI, channel contributions with patient-bootstrap CIs, and tested the plausibility of sizing effects in a follow-up-only simulation. Results : Categories disagreed in 43/258 patients (16.7%; Wilson 95% CI 12.6–21.7; Cohen κ = 0.76). Sizing contributed 8.3% (95% CI 5.0–11.8), detection/localization 5.2% (2.7–7.9), and false persistence 3.1% (1.2–5.4). Sizing exceeded persistence and omission separately, but not detection/localization combined (+3.1 percentage points, 95% CI −1.2 to 7.4); no channel clearly dominated. Multiple errors occurred in 13/43 disagreements (30%). Post hoc, 28 disagreements moved toward apparent benefit and 15 toward harm, but this pattern changed with target selection and did not test objective-response rate. Resampled sizing errors gave a 9.3% mean flip rate (central 95% simulation interval 6.2–12.4), which encompassed the 8.3% sizing contribution. Flip rates ranged from 15.5% to 18.6% across sensitivity analyses and from 15.0% to 18.4% across leave-one-fold-out subsets. Conclusions : Segmentation errors changed target-lesion response in about one in six patients. Measurement error was important but not clearly dominant. These findings concern follow-up errors from one prompt-assisted model, conditional on a correct expert baseline, in an internal out-of-fold evaluation. Independent confirmation is needed, especially for disagreement direction.

title: Clinical nodal findings and indocyanine green-guided sentinel node mapping in non-metastatic colon cancer: an exploratory prospective cohort stratified by postoperative mismatch-repair status
abstract: Abstract Background Nodal enlargement can be difficult to interpret in mismatch-repair-deficient (dMMR) colon cancer, and indocyanine green-guided sentinel lymph node biopsy (ICG-SLNB) can miss nodal metastases. We described clinical nodal findings and ICG-SLNB results by postoperative mismatch-repair (MMR) status. Methods This exploratory, non-consecutive single-centre cohort included 40 patients undergoing elective colectomy for clinically non-metastatic colon cancer (May 2024 to March 2026). One radiologist retrospectively reread all CT scans, blinded to final pathological nodal status (pN) and MMR status. Against final composite pN we evaluated a binary ≥ 5-mm nodal-enlargement marker (CT-LAP), a study-defined size and morphology composite (CT-MTS), intraoperative lymphadenopathy and ICG-SLNB. MMR comparisons used exploratory Fisher exact tests. All diagnostic and MMR-stratified analyses were exploratory. Results MMR was available for 38 patients (14 dMMR; 24 mismatch-repair-proficient [pMMR]). CT-LAP was present in 14/14 dMMR and 7/24 pMMR tumours (difference + 70.8 percentage points, 95% CI 41.4 to 85.1; exploratory p < 0.0001), whereas pN-positive disease occurred in 7/14 and 6/24 (difference + 25.0 points, 95% CI − 5.6 to + 51.6; exploratory p = 0.16). Among pN-negative tumours, CT-LAP specificity was 0/7 in dMMR and 15/18 in pMMR (difference − 83.3 points, 95% CI − 94.2 to − 41.3). CT-MTS sensitivity was 46.2% (6/13) and specificity 92.0% (23/25). Sentinel-node detection succeeded in 38/40 patients (95.0%) and 36 invasive tumours were evaluable. Among 12 pN-positive patients with successful SLN detection, sensitivity was 50.0% (6/12, 95% CI 25.4 to 74.6) and negative predictive value 80.0% (24/30, 95% CI 62.7 to 90.5). One additional pN-positive dMMR patient had SLN non-detection. Ultrastaging found isolated tumour cells in six patients, but no micrometastasis and no pN-positive upstaging among 24 pN-negative patients with successful SLN detection (upper 95% limit 13.8%). Conclusions Every dMMR patient had at least one regional node ≥ 5 mm, but CT-LAP did not discriminate pN status within the dMMR stratum, and sensitivity after SLN detection was 50% under the study-specific ICG protocol. Selection, sparse strata and phenotype imbalances prevent attribution to MMR status or transfer of these estimates, and clinical benefit was not assessed. Validation in a consecutive, prespecified MMR-stratified cohort is required before these observations inform practice. Trial registration: Not registered.

title: Prototype-aware Channel-Selective Spatial Interaction for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Semi-supervised 2D medical image segmentation reduces the dependence on dense pixel-level annotations by exploiting unlabeled images, but reliable learning remains challenging when only limited labeled data are available. Existing methods mainly rely on prediction-level consistency or generic feature interaction, and often lack explicit semantic guidance for selecting foreground-background discriminative channels and refining selected features at spatial locations. To address this issue, we propose Prototype-aware Channel-Selective Spatial Interaction (PCSI), a teacher-student framework for semi-supervised 2D medical image segmentation. PCSI constructs decoupled labeled and unlabeled foreground-background prototype memories, where reliable labeled prototypes provide semantic anchors and mature unlabeled prototypes gradually incorporate complementary distributional information. Based on prototype responses, PCSI selects a compact set of task-relevant channels according to foreground-background discriminability. Within this selected channel subspace, spatial feature tokens interact with category prototypes to obtain semantic residuals, which are injected into bottleneck features through confidence-gated residual enhancement. Extensive experiments on four public 2D medical image segmentation datasets under different labeled ratios demonstrate that PCSI consistently outperforms representative semi-supervised segmentation methods. These results indicate that prototype-aware, category-discriminative, and spatially adaptive feature interaction is effective for reliable semi-supervised medical image segmentation under limited annotation.

title: Fospropofol disodium injection as a sedative reduces hypoxemia and postinduction hypotension in patients undergoing painless gastrointestinal endoscopy: A prospective, randomized, controlled, multicenter clinical trial
abstract: Abstract Background With the growing popularity of comfortable medical care, patient demand for painless diagnostic and therapeutic procedures is also increasing. This study evaluated the efficacy and safety of fospropofol disodium injection as a sedative in patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopic examination or treatment. Methods This prospective, randomized, controlled, multicenter clinical study was conducted at five study centers between January 2025 and December 2025. A total of 426 patients aged 50–65 years, with a body mass index (BMI) of 18–28 kg/m², of either sex, classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I-II, and scheduled for elective gastrointestinal endoscopic examination or treatment were randomized to receive either fospropofol disodium or propofol. All patients received sufentanil (5 µg). One minute later, patients in the fospropofol disodium group received an intravenous bolus of fospropofol disodium (8 mg/kg), whereas those in the propofol group received an intravenous bolus of propofol (2 mg/kg) for sedation induction. The primary outcomes were the incidences of postinduction hypotension (PIH) and hypoxemia. Secondary outcomes included sedation induction time, sedation success rate at 5 minutes after induction, intraoperative patient movement, recovery time, length of stay in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU), hemodynamic variables, incidences of hypotension and bradycardia at each time point, use of vasoactive agents, and follow-up assessments of injection pain, paresthesia, and patient satisfaction. Results The fospropofol disodium group experienced significantly lower rates of PIH (4.22% vs 15.02%), hypoxemia (4.23% vs 17.37%), and injection pain, along with shorter PACU stays compared to the propofol group. However, their sedation success rate at 5 minutes post-induction was lower, with longer induction times, more body movement, and higher paresthesia incidence. Conclusions Fospropofol disodium injection provides stable respiratory and circulatory conditions and lowers the risk of PIH, hypoxemia, and injection pain during gastrointestinal endoscopy. Despite a longer induction time and less effective control of body movement, it does not increase other adverse effects, indicating its potential as a sedative for such procedures. Trial registration The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov before patient enrollment (NCT06732427; principal investigator: Yongtao Gao; registration date: December 06, 2024).

title: An Attention-Enhanced MobileViT Framework for Multi-Task Skin Lesion Classification and Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Deep learning-based automated skin lesion diagnosis has advanced substantially, but balancing diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency remains challenging for resource-constrained primary-care settings. Heavyweight segmentation and multi-task models deliver strong performance but carry prohibitive parameter overhead for practical deployment, while existing lightweight networks lack robust spatial feature enhancement and uncertainty constraints, limiting clinical diagnostic reliability. This work proposes an attention-augmented lightweight multi-task framework based on MobileViT-XS for joint skin lesion classification and semantic segmentation. The framework adopts MobileViT-XS as the shared backbone to extract multi-scale lesion features, integrates a convolutional block attention module (CBAM) to enhance lesion-related spatial representations under dense pixel-level supervision, and constructs a dual-branch multi-task architecture forming an asymmetric task promotion paradigm favoring classification optimization. A conservative prediction strategy coupled with risk stratification is further designed to mitigate overconfident outputs for ambiguous samples and improve diagnostic safety. Experiments on the ISIC 2019 dataset demonstrate that the proposed model achieves 84.37% accuracy, 79.46% Macro-F1, 0.935 Macro-AUC, 86.37% Dice coefficient, and 78.09% mIoU with only 2.62 M parameters. Overall, the proposed framework strikes a well-balanced trade-off among accuracy, computational efficiency, visual interpretability and clinical prediction safety, providing a deployable lightweight solution for primary-care skin lesion screening. title: Automated Whole-Lung CT Morphometric Phenotyping with Novel Shape Indices: A Pilot Study in Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Background Computed tomography (CT) lung cancer classification plays a crucial role in earlier diagnosis and thereby to offer better treatment to thep. Although radiomics makes it possible to analyse medical images quantitatively, most research only examines the tumour region of interest rather than the overall lung architecture. The factors like Atelectasis, comorbid airway disease, and tumor mass effect can even change the shape of the entire lung and in order to characterize global lung morphology beyond radiomic shape parameters, this pilot study is focused on two composite shape descriptors, the Shape Complexity Index (SCI) and the Axis Disparity Index (ADI), to quantify global lung morphology beyond radiomic shape features. Results A fully automated pipeline, integrating DICOM-to-NIfTI conversion, lobe-based lung segmentation using TotalSegmentator, and radiomic feature extraction with PyRadiomics, was implemented on CT series from eight patients in the TCGA-LUSC collection who satisfied predefined image quality criteria. In total, 107 standard radiomic features plus SCI and ADI were computed for each patient. Spearman correlation analysis showed that SCI and ADI captured morphological information that was largely non-redundant with conventional shape descriptors. Patients grouped by median SCI differed substantially in axis length and elongation, with a large effect size for SCI itself (Cohen's d = 1.18). Unsupervised K-means clustering on the shape-feature set, including SCI and ADI, identified two morphologically distinct phenotypes that separated clearly in principal component space. In leave-one-out cross-validated (LOOC) logistic regression using provisional, non-clinical outcome labels, a model combining conventional features with SCI and ADI achieved the same accuracy (0.625) and area under the curve (0.812) as a conventional-features-only baseline. This indicates that the additional biomarkers did not reduce classification performance in this small sample. Conclusions This feasibility study shows that an automated whole-lung morphometric pipeline is technically achievable and that SCI and ADI provide structural information that is largely distinct from standard radiomic shape features, without compromising classifier performance. Given the very small, single-cohort sample and provisional outcome labels, these findings are preliminary. Validation in larger, clinically annotated, multi-institutional cohorts is required before any diagnostic or prognostic claims can be made.

title: Patient Specific Three-dimensional Titanium Plate Versus Conventional Two Miniplate Fixation for Mandibular Angle Fractures: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: Abstract Background Mandibular angle fractures are clinically challenging because of their anatomical complexity and biomechanical loading. Conventional two miniplate fixation requires intraoperative plate adaptation and transbuccal instrumentation. Patient specific three-dimensional titanium plates may improve surgical efficiency. Objective This study aimed to clinically and radiographically evaluate patient specific three-dimensional titanium plate versus conventional two miniplates fixation in the management of mandibular angle fractures. Methods Sixteen patients with recent mandibular angle fractures were randomly allocated into two equal groups (n = 8). Group I underwent fixation using a patient specific three-dimensional titanium plate positioned according to the preoperative virtual plan, whereas Group II received conventional two miniplate fixation. The primary outcome was functional recovery assessed by maximal mouth opening (MMO). Secondary outcomes included operative time, postoperative pain intensity, facial edema, postoperative occlusion, wound healing, and radiographic bone healing assessed by computed tomography using bone density measurements in Hounsfield units (HU). Clinical outcomes were evaluated on postoperative days 1, 7, 14, and 30, whereas bone density was assessed immediately postoperatively and after 4 months. Results Operative time was significantly shorter in the patient specific plate group than in the conventional two miniplate group (40.00 ± 9.35 vs. 73.25 ± 11.22 min; P < 0.001). Pain intensity was significantly lower in the patient specific plate group on postoperative day 1 (P = 0.015), while facial edema was significantly lower on postoperative days 1 (P = 0.012) and 7 (P = 0.031). Both groups demonstrated satisfactory functional recovery and fracture healing, with no significant between group differences in maximal mouth opening, postoperative occlusion, Landry wound healing index scores, or bone density at the 4-month follow up. One patient in each group developed wound dehiscence, with complete healing after conservative management. Conclusions Patient specific three-dimensional titanium plates achieved clinical and radiographic outcomes comparable to conventional two miniplate fixation while significantly reducing operative time and improving early postoperative recovery through lower pain intensity and facial edema. These findings support the use of patient specific three-dimensional plates for the management of mandibular angle fractures. Trial registration: The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07390734) on 29 January 2026.

title: Differentiation of Benign and Malignant Musculoskeletal Tumors in Children Using MRI: A Clinico-Radiological Study
abstract: Abstract Purpose Accurate differentiation between benign and malignant musculoskeletal tumors in pediatric patients remains a significant diagnostic challenge due to overlapping clinical and imaging features. The aim of this study was to analyze clinical and MRI characteristics of musculoskeletal tumors and to develop a predictive model for malignancy. Materials and Methods This retrospective multicenter study included 113 pediatric patients (aged 5–19 years) with histologically confirmed musculoskeletal tumors. The cohort comprised 41 bone tumors and 72 soft tissue tumors. MRI features and clinical parameters were analyzed using statistical methods and logistic regression. Model performance was evaluated using ROC analysis, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and predictive values. Results Malignant tumors were significantly associated with larger size, irregular and ill-defined margins, heterogeneous internal structure, necrosis, invasion of surrounding tissues, and presence of a soft tissue component (p < 0.05). In bone tumors, malignant lesions were also associated with lytic bone destruction and aggressive periosteal reaction. The predictive model demonstrated high diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.933, sensitivity of 84.2%, specificity of 85.7%, and accuracy of 84.8%. Conclusion MRI-based evaluation combined with clinical parameters provides a reliable approach for differentiating benign and malignant musculoskeletal tumors in pediatric patients. The proposed model demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy and may serve as a useful decision-support tool in clinical practice. Trial registration Not applicable. This study is a retrospective observational study and was not registered as a clinical trial.

title: Clinical Evaluation of a Novel Artificial Intelligence-Based Image Processing Algorithm for Two-Dimensional Angiography
abstract: Abstract Background To evaluate the clinical performance of a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiographic imaging compared with its predecessor across multiple imaging modes, anatomic regions, and endovascular specialties. Materials and Methods This retrospective, comparative, randomized, paired, and blinded multicenter reader study included anonymized images acquired during clinically indicated endovascular interventions at 11 institutions in the United States and Europe. A total of 553 image series from 182 patients representing 51 procedure types across interventional radiology, neurointervention, cardiology, and pediatric cardiology were processed using both the AI-based and predecessor image processing algorithms. Thirteen board-certified physicians independently evaluated paired images using five-point Likert scales for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details. The primary endpoint was non-inferiority of overall image quality. Secondary endpoints evaluated superiority across image quality metrics using a predefined hierarchical testing strategy. Results The AI-based image processing algorithm demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality in 98.9% of all evaluations (95% confidence interval [CI], 98.0%–100.0%), meeting the primary endpoint across all imaging modes, anatomic regions, and predefined subgroups. Superiority of the AI-based algorithm was demonstrated for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details across fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. Overall image quality superiority was not demonstrated for digital subtraction angiography, likely reflecting the intrinsically higher signal-to-noise characteristics of these acquisitions. Inter-reader agreement analysis demonstrated identical ratings in 49.3% of evaluations, with 94.7% of paired ratings differing by no more than one Likert category. Conclusions In this multicenter blinded reader study, AI-based image processing demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality compared with its predecessor across all evaluated imaging modes and patient subgroups, with superior performance for multiple image quality metrics in fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. These findings support the clinical utility of AI-based image processing for endovascular imaging and provide a foundation for future studies evaluating its impact on radiation dose and procedural outcomes.

title: PSMASegmentator: Open-source, AI-based software for PSMA PET/CT automatic segmentation and prognostic biomarker extraction
abstract: Abstract Purpose: To develop and validate a fully-automated, Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool, PSMASegmentator, for the segmentation of Prostate Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA) PET/CT scans and extraction of imaging biomarkers. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 1035 PSMA PET/CT scans for training (Germany, n = 597; Australia, n = 438), with multicentre Australian testing datasets (internal, n = 199; external, n = 100). An nnU-Net–based deep learning model with PSMA-specific extensions was trained to segment PSMA-expressing lesions and derive biomarkers aligned with current consensus guidelines (total lesion count [TLC], total tumour volume [TTV], SUVmean, and SUVmax), plus total lesion uptake (TLU) and quotient (TLQ). Segmentation performance was evaluated primarily using F1 and Dice scores and the prognostic power of extracted biomarkers. The software was then executed on an external cohort (n = 1,282; 2015–2024) with linked mortality data. Biomarker value for survival prognosis was assessed in this cohort using Cox regression and Kaplan–Meier analysis. Results: Segmentation performance (n = 299 multicentre scans) was robust (lesion-level F1: 0.800; median Dice: 0.716) and generalisable (p > 0.05 between internal and external sets for F1 and Dice). Agreement between AI- and physician-derived biomarkers was high (Spearman’s ρ = 0.906–0.964; p Conclusion: PSMASegmentator, a freely available software (available at: https://github.com/UWA-Medical-Physics-Research-Group/PSMASegmentator), enables reproducible extraction of prognostically significant PSMA PET/CT biomarkers, facilitating standardised reporting aligned with consensus guidelines and hypothesis generation in research, clinical trials, and collaborative initiatives.

title: Multi-classification of Brain Tumor MRI images using Convoluted Neural Network (CNN) based approach
abstract: Abstract A brain tumor is considered a fatal condition, and a wrong diagnosis of the type and stage of the brain tumor will reduce the patient’s survival rate. Many malignancies, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), can be treated if detected early. Inspecting MRI scans is a convenient way of identifying brain tumors, but it is time consuming and can lead to human errors due to the enormous amount of data. To address this issue, different deep learning methods are used in literature for identification and categorization of various types of cancers, allowing doctors to plan treatment. In this study, we have proposed a model that uses a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for the classification of brain tumors into Glioma, Meningioma, Pituitary and absentia (no tumor or normal condition). CNN is a deep learning algorithm built primarily for tasks that require object recognition, such as picture categorization, detection, and segmentation. The suggested model incorporates 7 convolutional layers with different kernel sizes, and ReLU is utilized as an activation function. Model was trained and tested on a publicly available dataset on Kaggle. The dataset consists of 7023 images, 5712 images for training and 1311 for testing. Using our simple architecture without any pre-trained model, we have achieved a training accuracy of 99.71%, a validation accuracy of 96.06% and a test accuracy of 96.10%. These results significantly demonstrate robustness of the proposed model and shows promising performance for computer-aided diagnosis. The model outperformed the existing comparative models for automated brain tumour detection and warrants further clinical validation.

title: Automated 3D CT Segmentation of Intercostal Muscles Using Bayesian U-Net: a retrospective technical validation study with exploratory pulmonary function analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Quantitative evaluation of respiratory muscles is increasingly important in thoracic imaging, yet intercostal muscles remain difficult to assess on computed tomography (CT) because of their thin, curved anatomy. We developed a Bayesian U-Net-based method for automated 3D intercostal muscle segmentation on thin-slice chest CT and explored associations between CT-derived muscle metrics and pulmonary function. Methods This retrospective technical validation study included 145 chest CT examinations: 129 from patients undergoing pulmonary tumor surgery for model development/internal validation and 16 from another institution for external validation. An uncertainty-based active-learning framework produced 60 manually corrected reference examinations. Segmentation performance was assessed using fivefold cross-validation and independent external validation against two reader-generated ground truth labels, including an additional full-volume validation of the bilateral sixth intercostal muscles. Associations with pulmonary function were evaluated in 95 examinations using Pearson correlation and exploratory multivariable linear regression adjusted for height, body mass index, age, and sex. Results Internal validation showed a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.84 ± 0.08 and an average symmetric surface distance (ASSD) of 0.66 +/- 0.47 mm. In external validation, DSC values were 0.774 ± 0.043 and 0.796 ± 0.045 versus the two ground truth labels, comparable to the interobserver DSC of 0.775 ± 0.042. For the bilateral sixth intercostal muscles, DSC was 0.738 ± 0.025, ASSD was 0.921 ± 0.161 mm, and 95-percentile Housdorff distance (HD95) was 2.673 ± 0.220 mm. Intercostal muscle volume correlated positively with forced vital capacity (FVC; r = 0.568) and forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1; r = 0.429). In exploratory adjusted analyses, total and lean intercostal muscle volumes remained positively associated with FVC, whereas the FEV1 association was attenuated. Conclusions Automated 3D segmentation of intercostal muscles on thin-slice chest CT is technically feasible. CT-derived intercostal muscle metrics showed biologically plausible exploratory associations with pulmonary function, particularly FVC, supporting future disease-focused respiratory muscle imaging studies.

title: Lightweight attention mechanisms in breast ultrasound lesion segmentation: parameter cost, protocol choice, data leakage, and what the data can resolve
abstract: Abstract Background. Reported segmentation results on the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset span a wide range, and the protocols behind them differ in ways not always stated. Whether the architectural differences those results support are large enough to be resolved by the data has not been established. Methods. We trained eleven U-Net variants under a single evaluation protocol on the 647 lesion-bearing images, using three independent random splits (Monte Carlo cross-validation) with a held-out test partition separate from validation, and computed all metrics from stored masks with one evaluation module. Five attention mechanisms were compared against a common reference and four ablation-axis steps as a separate family, each corrected for multiplicity within its family. For every comparison we report a minimum detectable effect from that comparison's own paired differences, with standard errors on independent clusters rather than images. Parameter cost was counted from the trained model files. Results. Parameter cost spanned three orders of magnitude across the five mechanisms (12 to 32,595 parameters in the deployed model) while measured gains spanned 0.0020 to 0.0137 Dice. The largest gain came from the cheapest mechanism, efficient channel attention with deep supervision, at 12 parameters. No gain reached the threshold its own comparison could resolve; the largest was 0.52 of a multiplicity-corrected threshold of 0.0262, with win rates between 49.1 % and 56.4 %. Network depth, by contrast, produced a resolved effect of +0.0400. Selecting the reported checkpoint on the evaluation partition rather than a held-out one moved the reported value by +0.0316 to +0.0355 in our own runs. A published lightweight baseline exceeded the best ablation configuration by +0.0150, a margin that its own comparison could not resolve either. An audit of the distributed dataset found 146 near-duplicate pairs; removing them moved absolute Dice by 0.0203 but paired differences by 0.0065. Conclusions. On this benchmark the parameter cost of an attention module and the effect it produces are not aligned, and the effects lie below what the data can resolve. We report these magnitudes so that the cost of an architectural decision can be weighed against the evidence for its benefit.

An audit of the distributed dataset found 146 near-duplicate pairs; removing them moved absolute Dice by 0.0203 but paired differences by 0.0065. Conclusions. On this benchmark the parameter cost of an attention module and the effect it produces are not aligned, and the effects lie below what the data can resolve. We report these magnitudes so that the cost of an architectural decision can be weighed against the evidence for its benefit.

title: BCSDBT-Seg Lesion Segmentation Annotations and Structured BI-RADS Reports for Breast Tomosynthesis Dataset
abstract: Abstract Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) is an established imaging modality for breast cancer screening that reduces tissue overlap compared with conventional digital mammography. Publicly available DBT datasets remain scarce, and existing resources predominantly provide coarse image-level labels or 2D bounding boxes. Here, we present BCSDBT-Seg, an open-access, expert-annotated dataset providing 3D voxel-level lesion segmentation masks and structured clinical reports for the publicly available Breast Cancer Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis (BCS-DBT) collection. Radiologists manually delineated lesion boundaries on 396 DBT volumes (craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views) from 201 biopsy-confirmed patients, yielding 434 distinct lesion masks. In addition, structured Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) descriptors, breast density ratings, and pathology outcomes are provided per case. Technical validation using 3D nnU-Net baseline models demonstrates the quality and utility of the annotations. BCSDBT-Seg supports applications in automated segmentation, radiomics, and deep learning model development for breast image analysis.

title: Toward uncertainty-aware clinical decision support for treatment response prediction in metastatic NSCLC: integrating FDG-PET, T-cell repertoire, and cytokines with conformal prediction
abstract: Abstract Background Variable response to chemoimmunotherapy in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (mNSCLC), together with the limited discriminative accuracy of PD-L1 tumor proportion score, highlights the need for reliable, uncertainty-aware early response prediction using multimodal biomarkers. We developed and prototyped a multimodal clinical decision support (CDS) framework integrating longitudinal FDG-PET, T-cell receptor (TCR), and cytokine biomarkers with conformal prediction to deliver uncertainty-quantified, patient-level response predictions. Methods Thirty-five patients with mNSCLC receiving first-line carboplatin–pemetrexed–pembrolizumab on the PET-BRIGHT trial (NCT04151940) underwent FDG-PET/CT and blood collection at baseline and week 3. Multimodal biomarkers included FDG-PET metrics (standardized uptake value/total lesion glycolysis), TCR diversity metrics, and inflammatory cytokines. Nested leave-one-out cross-validation with automated feature selection identified a single biomarker per modality. Class-balanced logistic regression was used for classification, with discrimination assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration by the Brier score. Conformal prediction (targeting 80% reliability) quantified patient-level uncertainty via prediction sets and singleton rate. Unimodal and multimodal early- and late-fusion models were evaluated using baseline-only and combined baseline plus mid-treatment biomarkers. Models were benchmarked against PD-L1 tumor proportion score, and statistical significance was assessed by permutation testing against an empirical null. Results PD-L1 tumor proportion score, the current clinical standard, discriminated poorly (AUROC 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.78). At PreTx, unimodal TCR was the strongest single modality (AUROC 0.80), followed by PET (0.76) and cytokines (0.54). Late fusion of PET and TCR achieved the highest PreTx discrimination (0.85) and increased singleton predictions from 78% to 89%. After incorporating mid-treatment biomarkers, cytokines became the strongest single modality (0.78) while TCR was attenuated (0.66); late fusion of PET and cytokines achieved the highest discrimination overall (0.86). Thirteen of 22 model and timepoint combinations exceeded a permutation null at p < 0.05, and empirical coverage was 78% and 82% against an 80% target. Conclusions A multimodal framework combining longitudinal biomarkers with conformal prediction substantially outperformed the current clinical standard while identifying patients for whom a confident prediction could not be made. A prototype CDS interface demonstrates feasibility for clinical translation. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04151940, registered 26 September 2019.

title: Stakeholders’ perceptions of AI-assisted obstetric ultrasound in rural and urban Kenya: a qualitative study
abstract: Abstract Introduction : As artificial intelligence (AI) tools gain popularity in maternal healthcare, understanding community and health system perspectives is essential for inclusive and ethical implementation. This study explores stakeholder views on AI-supported ultrasound for pregnancy care in Kenya, that emphasized trust, equity, system readiness, and the importance of community engagement. Methods : A qualitative study was conducted in two Kenyan settings: Nairobi (urban) and Kilifi County (rural). Fifty-five semi-structured interviews and three focus group discussions were conducted with pregnant women, partners, healthcare providers, Sub-County Health Management Teams (SCHMTs), Community Health Promoters (CHPs), and community and religious leaders. Data were analyzed inductively using grounded theory principles. Results : The participants viewed AI with cautious optimism. While many welcomed its potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and access, concerns emerged around data privacy, informed consent, quality of care, and over-automation. Reliability or trust was linked to transparency, human oversight, and the use of local data. Participants highlighted structural challenges, including weak referral systems and staffing gaps, raising questions about the health system’s readiness to integrate AI. Fears of equity and “pilotitis”, short-lived projects without sustainability, were also expressed. Conclusion: Findings from this study suggest that AI implementation in maternal health may need to go beyond technology development and deployment. Developers and relevant stakeholders may need to consider co-designing with communities, alignment with health system realities, and the integration of ethical principles such as equity, accountability, and transparency.

title: Risk Aware Prompt-Guided CNN–LLM Framework for Brain MRI Diagnostic Report Generation
abstract: Abstract Brain MRI report generation has emerged as a core task for AI-aided radiology, which could potentially fill the gap of low efficiency among radiologists in tumour diagnosis. Yet, current methods are often too weak to fully express the clinical variances in disease and anatomical regions, which results in repetitive genetic reports. To overcome such limitations, the proposed a risk-aware prompt-based medical report generation framework that utilizes the vision-based deep visual perception and Large Language Models (LLMs) to produce brain tumour reports that are accurate and clinically interpretable. This work proposes a semantic prompt engineering framework based on prediction scores and latent semantic embeddings obtained from an CNN-based (Convolutional Neural Networks) tumour classifier. These prompts also utilize improved context and uncertainty aware learning state embeddings as to balance the representation of diagnostic cues and counteract biases over the dominant tumour types. A special prompt selection module, trained by feedback-weighted adaptation with radiologist feedback, acts as a contextual mediator, mapping a classifier's predictions to section-based medical reporting schemas that are compatible with radiological reasoning. Moreover, the suggested work is among the first to include feedback-based adaptation loop with a radiologist, jointly refining the visual and language components based on expert feedback, facilitating learning on the fly and improved alignment to clinical need. This is supported by comprehensive experiments on a curated brain MRI dataset, demonstrating that the proposed framework outperforms conventional classification metrics by a large margin in terms of report quality and clinical consistency, and hence is applicable in practical healthcare settings
